A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ERDM research, despite the broader title in v2. Their main text and complete Appendices A-F, including algorithms, equations, figures and tables, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Navier-Stokes and ERA5 forecasting experiments, including skill, calibration, ablations, spectral analyses and forecast visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds PDE-Refiner evaluation results and measured computational-efficiency results.

M1.justification: Section 4, Algorithms 1-3 and Appendix C retain the same progressive noise schedule, loss weighting, preconditioning, external initialization, temporal architecture and sampling procedures. Expanded baseline explanations and limitations do not change ERDM.

E1.justification: Both evaluate four-obstacle Navier-Stokes forecasting and 1.5-degree ERA5 weather forecasting with the same variables and horizons. The 2022 evaluation-year analysis and forecast examples already appear in v1; no new dataset, domain or forecasting scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: PDE-Refiner moves from cited related work in v1 to an evaluated Navier-Stokes comparator in v2, appearing in Figure 4 alongside DYffusion and the EDM variants. The existing weather comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The new efficiency benchmark uses one A100 GPU, mixed precision, a 15-day, 30-step, five-member forecast with Heun sampling, and batch size one for training-memory measurements. These are additional profiling conditions; the existing forecasting splits, metrics, training settings and evaluation ensemble sizes are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.5 adds a supplementary analysis testing whether fewer neural function evaluations translate into lower runtime and memory costs. The existing design-choice ablations, initialization comparisons, evaluation-year sensitivity study and spectral analyses are unchanged; v1 Table 1 becomes v2 Table 2 with identical results.

E5.justification: Both report three random training seeds for the Navier-Stokes baselines and retain the uncertainty bands for existing comparisons. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated-run counts or uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds PDE-Refiner results showing strong initial skill but worse long-range performance and calibration than ERDM. New Table 1 reports EDM versus ERDM at 600 versus 120 NFEs, 237 versus 209 seconds, and 21 versus 49 GB inference memory. Existing forecasting curves and ablation values remain; Table 3 summarizes existing Figure 10 results.

T1.justification: The mathematical construction, SDE/ODE derivations, preconditioning formulas, temporal noise prior and metric definitions in the main text and Appendices B-D are retained. Typesetting and citation changes do not revise the mathematical content.

C1.justification: Despite the broader title and rewritten conclusion, both versions claim the same rolling-EDM integration, loss weighting, initialization strategy and temporal architecture, with long-range forecasting advantages on Navier-Stokes and ERA5. The new efficiency measurements support existing claims rather than redefine the contributions.

C2.justification: The new limitations paragraph identifies memory as a barrier to higher-resolution scaling, external-initializer dependence, and possible disadvantages of explicit loss weighting versus importance sampling. Section 5.3 additionally attributes short-range weaknesses to a backbone not specialized for weather, while Appendix D.3 offers an explanation for PDE-Refiner's deterioration.

D1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds PDE-Refiner tuning details, including K=6 and sigma_min=0.002, and clarifies the existing multi-frame EDM rollout procedure. Section 5.5 documents profiling conditions. The stated code repository changes from salvaRC/erdm to NVlabs/ERDM, and the forecast-video access location also changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to ArchesWeather/ArchesWeatherGen, PreDiff, Diffusion Probabilistic Modeling for Video Generation, and Noise Schedules Considered Harmful. Related work now mentions flow matching, while the central positioning relative to EDM and rolling diffusion remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 broadens the title to complex-dynamics forecasting, edits the abstract, introduction and results discussion, and rewrites the conclusion. It adds a computational-complexity subsection and an explicit limitations paragraph, while retaining the overall methodological and appendix organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds efficiency Table 1 and selected-CRPS Table 3, renumbers the unchanged ablation table, and adds PDE-Refiner curves and a legend entry to Figure 4. Appendix figures are locally rearranged; the remaining embedded graphics are unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added PDE-Refiner comparison and measured runtime-memory tradeoff strengthen empirical support and transparency. Clearer baseline documentation and specific limitations also improve interpretation, while the method and most evidence remain unchanged. Table 3 introduces a small labeling inconsistency, with ten days in its caption but fourteen-day columns, which does not outweigh these limited benefits.
